=== overpaid
# Overpaid: household overpayments and the law behind each one

Status: proposed, 7 November 2026.

## Idea

A household uploads its bills. The app finds each recurring charge where it pays more than it should, names the rule that backs a complaint, and drafts a letter citing it. For broadband and mobile, that's Ofcom's rule that price rises in new contracts must be stated in pounds and pence. For insurance, it's the FCA's 2022 ban on charging renewing customers more than new ones. For rent, it's illegal fees under the Rent (Scotland) Act 1984. For energy, it uses Octopus Agile half-hourly prices and grid carbon intensity to say when to run appliances, and whether Agile beats a fixed tariff.

## Origin

Raised by an AI agent as "Loyalty Tax" in a brainstorm on 7 November 2026, at macmac's request. The agent was extending the team's mispricing ideas to the household side. In the debate round its advocate merged it with the renting idea that became [Flat Truth](flat-truth.md). A judge agent ranked it fifth and found it weaker than Flat Truth on every track they share (see [idea-ranking.md](../idea-ranking.md)).

## Evidence and data

- Confirmed in agents' web checks on 7 November 2026: the Octopus and carbon intensity APIs are open and need no key.

## Tracks it could serve

- Bank of Scotland: strong. It covers cost, time, convenience and sustainability.
- Wordsmith: moderate. It reads contract terms and cites rules, but the browser part is thin.
- G-Research: moderate. The hidden thing is the loyalty penalty.
- HRT: weak to moderate. It forecasts energy prices, but Octopus already publishes the next day's prices at about 4pm.

## Challenges it could use

=== unclaimed-money
# Unclaimed: the money you never claimed

Status: proposed, 7 November 2026.

## Idea

A person describes their circumstances: where they live, who is in the household, their income, whether they rent, their age and any children. A browser agent then checks the entitlement rules that apply across the UK and works out what they can claim. That covers council tax reduction from their own council's scheme in England, Scotland or Wales, rate relief in Northern Ireland, the devolved Scottish benefits such as the Scottish Child Payment and the Best Start grants, the Scottish Welfare Fund, the Warm Home Discount, water charges reduction, and social tariffs for broadband and phone.

It returns two things. First, a total of what is going unclaimed, split into weekly and yearly. Second, the claim itself: the agent fills each application form with the details it already has, attaches the documents each one asks for, and stops before submitting so the person reviews the lot. It is for households on low or fixed incomes who do not know what exists, or who gave up on the forms.

## Origin

Raised by an AI agent on 7 November 2026, in a brainstorm at macmac's request. It came after the user ruled out career prizes and asked for ideas that fit the sponsor tracks better than the first ten. The market was checked on 7 November 2026; the other facts are unchecked.

## Existing products

- **Inbest** (Edinburgh, founded 2016) is the closest company. It sells a white-label benefits calculator as an API and an embeddable widget, and it runs inside the **Lloyds, Halifax and Bank of Scotland** apps. In May 2025 the Money and Pensions Service contracted it to power the government's MoneyHelper benefits checker. Its case-management system is a tool for welfare and debt advisers, not an agent that files claims. ([Inbest](https://inbest.ai/), [PublicTechnology](https://www.publictechnology.net/2025/05/13/society-and-welfare/dwp-body-to-deploy-white-label-commercial-tool-for-government-online-benefits-calculator/))
- **Turn2us**, **EntitledTo**, **Policy in Practice**, **MoneyHelper**, gov.scot and Citizens Advice all give the discovery step away free. The estimate is a commodity.
- **IncomeMax** is a UK social enterprise that does the claiming step with people: advisers complete forms, make advocacy calls and challenge decisions, and it is partnered with EDF Energy. The same job, delivered as human labour. ([IncomeMax](https://www.incomemax.org.uk/))
- Hackathon versions of the discovery step exist: **Benefits-Finder** (DevFest Columbia 2026), **MyAutoBenefits**, **MamaPal**, and the COVID-19 California Benefits Finder. ([Benefits-Finder](https://devfest-2026.devpost.com/project-gallery?page=2))

What is not a product: one agent that takes a household's details, tests them against several unrelated schemes, and completes each application form itself. No UK company found doing that. The nearest precedent is **DoNotPay** in the US, which promised an AI that filled forms and disputed charges; the FTC fined it $193,000 in 2024, finalised in February 2025, for claiming untested capabilities and barred it from presenting itself as a lawyer substitute. ([FTC](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/02/ftc-finalizes-order-donotpay-prohibits-deceptive-ai-lawyer-claims-imposes-monetary-relief-requires))

So the idea is not new at either end, but the middle is unbuilt. The pitch has to be "the calculator exists, the claim does not get filed", and the demo has to show forms being completed, because that is the only part a Bank of Scotland judge cannot already find in the sponsor's own app.

=== cheap-hours
# Cheap Hours: the hidden half-hourly price of electricity

Status: proposed, 7 November 2026.

## Idea

Electricity has a real price every half hour, set by the wholesale market, and a carbon cost that changes too. Households on a flat tariff never see either. The app forecasts Octopus Agile prices and grid carbon intensity for the next few days. It tells you when to run the washing machine, charge an EV or heat the house, and whether a time-of-use tariff beats your fixed one. An optional browser agent reads your current supplier's terms and compares tariffs.

## Origin

Raised independently by two AI agents in a brainstorm on 7 November 2026, at macmac's request, as "Switch or Stay" and "Cheap Hours". It was not debated on its own, but its data was checked under [Overpaid](overpaid.md). Ranked ninth in [idea-ranking.md](../idea-ranking.md).

## Evidence and data

These come from agents' web checks on 7 November 2026.

- Confirmed with live calls: the Octopus API (Agile rates for South Scotland since October 2024, and postcode to region) and the carbon intensity API (regional, with 48-hour forecasts) are open and need no key.
- Octopus publishes the next day's prices at about 4pm.

## Existing products

- Community forecasters of Agile prices already exist (agents' web checks, 7 November 2026).

## Tracks it could serve

=== delay-compensation
# Delay compensation: file the claim you are owed

Status: proposed, 7 November 2026.

## Idea

A person enters a journey they have taken, or forwards the ticket email. An agent works out whether the train or flight was late enough to qualify, which scheme applies, and how much is owed. For rail that means the operator's Delay Repay threshold, which varies by operator. For flights it means UK261, where the distance and delay decide the band.

It then files the claim: it finds the right operator's form, fills it with the booking reference and journey details, attaches the ticket, and stops before submit. It also watches upcoming journeys and warns when a claim has just become possible, because most people never check.

## Origin

Raised by an AI agent on 7 November 2026, in a brainstorm at macmac's request, after the user ruled out career prizes and asked for ideas that fit the sponsor tracks better than the first ten. The market was checked on 7 November 2026; the other facts are unchecked.

## Existing products

- The category is saturated with fee-taking startups: **Claim Bot** (35% of the refund, scans the inbox), **SmartDelay** (25%), **Railed** (10%), **fare-ly** (10%, since 2019), **DelayRepay.uk**, **DelayDog** (TfL and National Rail) and **Latetrain**, plus **AirHelp**, **Flightright** and **EUclaim** for flights. **Untap** covers trains, flights, TfL overcharges and parking notices, drafts the claim and lets the user send it, and takes no cut. ([Claim Bot](https://www.claimsbot.ai/), [Untap](https://untap.money/))
- Hackathons: **GOOBus DeComS**, entered as "Delay Compensation for the people, by the people", won at LeedsHack 2025. **AirFair**, **Flight Delay**, **Refund Hunter** and **Points Failure** are on Devpost. ([LeedsHack 2025](https://leedshack2025.devpost.com/project-gallery))

Every part of the idea already exists: the entitlement calculation, the proactive monitoring, the form filling and the fee model. One version has already won a hackathon. The only remaining angle is doing it without taking a cut, which is a business-model difference rather than a product one.

## Tracks it could serve

- Bank of Scotland: strong. It is money recovered from an everyday cost, with the only trade-off being the time it takes to claim. The brief's cost-and-time framing fits directly.
- G-Research: strong. The hidden thing is that a delay already incurred has become a claim worth money. It is found by matching real running data against each operator's threshold, and it enables a payout nobody bothers to collect.

# Product

## What it is

The ad channel mispricing finder tells a startup where to advertise to reach its customers for less than the channels its competitors crowd into. A startup fills in a short form about its product, customer, budget and markets. It gets back a ranked list of specific placements, such as a particular airport's jet bridges, a students' union's media pack or a niche newsletter. Each comes with a real price and contact, a cost comparison against Meta, a way to measure results, and a drafted enquiry to the seller.

It is for startups that want customers beyond Meta and Google but have no media agency and a limited budget.

Three things set it apart from AI media planners and ad marketplaces:

- It discovers placements for each startup instead of choosing from a fixed catalogue, and it leaves out channels the startup's competitors already buy.
- It ranks placements by cost per thousand attentive seconds weighted by audience value, not by cost per thousand impressions. The source behind the idea shows the ranking flips: Berlin Brandenburg's jet bridges are about 9% dearer than Meta per impression but 2.78 times cheaper per attentive second, assuming four seconds of attention.
- It checks every placement against a real rate card or contact, and marks it unverified when it can't find one.

## Decisions

Every decision the user makes or confirms, including ones reported from teammates: who the product serves, data sources, methods or models, the stack, how parts connect, and the demo scope. Track and challenge priorities are recorded in `AGENTS.md`, not here. One line each: the decision, the reason, and the date. A changed decision is updated in place, so this section always describes the current plan.

- Product idea: the ad channel mispricing finder, which finds advertising channels that are underpriced for the attention and audience they deliver; details in `ideas/ad-channel-mispricing.md`. The user chose it over the other brainstormed ideas. 2026-11-07.
- Web app: Next.js 16 (App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, ESLint) managed with pnpm, in the `web/` folder rather than the repo root. The repo root stays for docs and agent config, and a second service such as a Python API can sit beside `web/` later. 2026-11-07.
- Frontend UI: shadcn/ui components styled with Tailwind CSS v4. 2026-11-07.
- LLM calls and AI agents: Vercel AI SDK. 2026-11-07.
- Recommend specific placements, such as Hamburg Airport's jet bridges, not mediums such as "airports". Per impression, airports as a medium are no cheaper than Meta (BER's jet bridges cost £14.24 per thousand against Meta's £13.02), so any underpricing is in individual placements, and a placement is something a startup can actually buy. 2026-11-07.
- The pipeline has six steps: crowded-channel check, candidates, gap filter, verification by per-medium agents, pricing, then report and outreach. Details in `plan/architecture-sketch.md`. 2026-11-07.
- Per-medium expert agents, such as an airport agent or a student union agent, verify candidates rather than propose them. Each medium is sold differently, and without a check the model invents plausible channels that don't exist or have no price. 2026-11-07.
- Placements are ranked by cost per thousand attentive seconds, weighted by audience value, against a Meta baseline, shown beside cost per thousand impressions. Attention seconds and the Meta price are sliders with the breakeven point marked, because no attention data exists for most placements. 2026-11-07.
- A channel counts as crowded if competitors advertise there, found through ad transparency libraries such as Meta's Ad Library and Google's Ads Transparency Center, or if we have already recommended it to another client in the same category. Recommending what similar startups use would send every client to the channels where competition has already raised prices. 2026-11-07.
- The onboarding form asks for industry, a one-sentence description, a one-sentence target customer, what a customer pays, monthly advertising budget, and markets. It does not ask B2B or B2C, which the target customer covers. Budget filters out placements with minimum spends, and what a customer pays stands in for lifetime value in the audience weighting because it is easier to answer. 2026-11-07.
- Every recommendation comes with a way to measure it, such as a QR code, promo code or landing page, because marketers avoid channels they can't measure. 2026-11-07.
- Data for one group of channels is gathered ahead of time with scripts in `tools/`, and the live agents add to it. A recorded run of the full pipeline is kept as a fallback for the demo, because live browser agents fail on cookie banners, PDFs and slow sites. 2026-11-07.

=== product.md
# Product

## What it is

The ad channel mispricing finder tells a startup where to advertise to reach its customers for less than the channels its competitors crowd into. A startup fills in a short form about its product, customer, budget and markets. It gets back a ranked list of specific placements, such as a particular airport's jet bridges, a students' union's media pack or a niche newsletter. Each comes with a real price and contact, a cost comparison against Meta, a way to measure results, and a drafted enquiry to the seller.

It is for startups that want customers beyond Meta and Google but have no media agency and a limited budget.

Three things set it apart from AI media planners and ad marketplaces:

- It discovers placements for each startup instead of choosing from a fixed catalogue, and it leaves out channels the startup's competitors already buy.
- It ranks placements by cost per thousand attentive seconds weighted by audience value, not by cost per thousand impressions. The source behind the idea shows the ranking flips: Berlin Brandenburg's jet bridges are about 9% dearer than Meta per impression but 2.78 times cheaper per attentive second, assuming four seconds of attention.
- It checks every placement against a real rate card or contact, and marks it unverified when it can't find one.

## Decisions

Every decision the user makes or confirms, including ones reported from teammates: who the product serves, data sources, methods or models, the stack, how parts connect, and the demo scope. Track and challenge priorities are recorded in `AGENTS.md`, not here. One line each: the decision, the reason, and the date. A changed decision is updated in place, so this section always describes the current plan.

- Product idea: the ad channel mispricing finder, which finds advertising channels that are underpriced for the attention and audience they deliver; details in `ideas/ad-channel-mispricing.md`. The user chose it over the other brainstormed ideas. 2026-11-07.
- Web app: Next.js 16 (App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, ESLint) managed with pnpm, in the `web/` folder rather than the repo root. The repo root stays for docs and agent config, and a second service such as a Python API can sit beside `web/` later. 2026-11-07.
- Frontend UI: shadcn/ui components styled with Tailwind CSS v4. 2026-11-07.
- LLM calls and AI agents: Vercel AI SDK. 2026-11-07.
- Recommend specific placements, such as Hamburg Airport's jet bridges, not mediums such as "airports". Per impression, airports as a medium are no cheaper than Meta (BER's jet bridges cost £14.24 per thousand against Meta's £13.02), so any underpricing is in individual placements, and a placement is something a startup can actually buy. 2026-11-07.
- The pipeline has six steps: crowded-channel check, candidates, gap filter, verification by per-medium agents, pricing, then report and outreach. Details in `plan/architecture-sketch.md`. 2026-11-07.
- Per-medium expert agents, such as an airport agent or a student union agent, verify candidates rather than propose them. Each medium is sold differently, and without a check the model invents plausible channels that don't exist or have no price. 2026-11-07.
- Placements are ranked by cost per thousand attentive seconds, weighted by audience value, against a Meta baseline, shown beside cost per thousand impressions. Attention seconds and the Meta price are sliders with the breakeven point marked, because no attention data exists for most placements. 2026-11-07.
- A channel counts as crowded if competitors advertise there, found through ad transparency libraries such as Meta's Ad Library and Google's Ads Transparency Center, or if we have already recommended it to another client in the same category. Recommending what similar startups use would send every client to the channels where competition has already raised prices. 2026-11-07.
- The onboarding form asks for industry, a one-sentence description, a one-sentence target customer, what a customer pays, monthly advertising budget, and markets. It does not ask B2B or B2C, which the target customer covers. Budget filters out placements with minimum spends, and what a customer pays stands in for lifetime value in the audience weighting because it is easier to answer. 2026-11-07.
- Every recommendation comes with a way to measure it, such as a QR code, promo code or landing page, because marketers avoid channels they can't measure. 2026-11-07.
- Data for one group of channels is gathered ahead of time with scripts in `tools/`, and the live agents add to it. A recorded run of the full pipeline is kept as a fallback for the demo, because live browser agents fail on cookie banners, PDFs and slow sites. 2026-11-07.

## Data sources

The rules come from four tiers, each with a different reliability and access method.

- **National law and guidance.** GOV.UK's Content and Search APIs return published pages as JSON without a key, and legislation.gov.uk has an API for the statutes and regulations behind them. Social Security Scotland and mygov.scot publish the devolved benefits, and nidirect publishes the Northern Ireland equivalents.
- **Local schemes.** About 350 councils run their own council tax reduction scheme: 296 billing authorities in England, 32 in Scotland and 22 in Wales. Each publishes a scheme document and its own application form. Local welfare assistance schemes are separate again and vary by council. Northern Ireland has no council tax; help with rates is Rate Relief and Rate Rebate, run by Land & Property Services and applied for through nidirect.
- **Supplier schemes.** Ofcom publishes the list of broadband and phone social tariffs with prices and coverage. Water companies publish their own reduction schemes, and the Warm Home Discount is administered through energy suppliers.
- **Eligibility engines.** EntitledTo, Inbest and Policy in Practice sell APIs that already encode Universal Credit and the legacy means-tested benefits, including the earnings taper, childcare and housing elements. Inbest is the awkward one, because it is the product already inside the Bank of Scotland app.

How the data is used:

- A rules store holds one entry per scheme: jurisdiction, eligibility conditions, award formula, evidence needed, application URL, source URL and effective date. Every entry carries a quotation from the source, so the product can show why a figure is owed.

- A re-fetch job diffs the pages and flags changes, because rates change each April and council schemes change annually.
- A postcode router picks the nation, then the council, then the schemes. The four nations do not share a system: Scotland has devolved benefits that England and Wales do not, and Northern Ireland uses rates relief.
- The claim layer is one adapter per portal, because the fields, login and evidence upload differ. Identity is the wall: most portals need a Government Gateway, MyScotGov or council account, and the claimant signs a declaration. The agent can fill and stop; it cannot create a verified account or sign.

The honest scope: the rules layer can cover all four nations, but the form layer cannot cover 350 councils in a weekend. The buildable version is all-UK rules with depth in Scotland, where the sponsor and the devolved benefits are, and a small number of real form adapters.

## Tracks it could serve

- Bank of Scotland: strong. This is the most direct fit of any idea so far. The brief is about everyday trade-offs between cost, time, convenience and sustainability, and this is money a household is already entitled to, with no trade-off except the effort of claiming. "Better" is defined by the household: more money, or the same money for less work.
- Wordsmith: strong. It is legal and administrative work, which Wordsmith prefers, and the workflow is longer than a read-only report: read circumstances, test them against a dozen rule sets, pick the schemes that apply, gather evidence, fill several unrelated forms with different fields, and stop before submit. Tokens, model and time should be shown, since Wordsmith also judges those.
- G-Research: strong. The hidden thing is money sitting unclaimed, found by cross-checking a household against eligibility rules that are scattered across councils and agencies, and it enables a claim worth hundreds or thousands a year. It answers the brief's three questions without needing a scrape of a site that may block us.
- HRT: weak. There is no market data and no real-time signal. At most, the entitlement rules could be modelled as a decision tree over a synthetic population, which is not what the track asks for.

## Challenges it could use

- Gemini API: reading council schemes and application forms, and driving the browser agent.
- Auth0: keeping a household's details and saved claims between sessions.
- Vultr: hosting the backend and the demo, separate from the browser runner.

## Open problems

These are unchecked, apart from the market check above.

- The total unclaimed is reported in the billions of pounds a year, but the figure, its source and its date are unverified. Do not cite a number until it is checked.
- The rules are genuinely complex and differ by council: about 350 councils run their own council tax reduction scheme, and the schemes change yearly. A wrong answer here is harmful in a way a wrong rent estimate is not, so the product should show which rule produced each figure and link to the source.
- Universal Credit is a means test with an earnings taper, childcare and housing elements. Rebuilding it is not a 24-hour job, and an LLM doing the arithmetic will be wrong. Use an eligibility engine, or hand-code a small set of schemes for the demo.
- Differentiation is the main risk. See Existing products: the Bank of Scotland app already contains Inbest's calculator, so the demo must show the forms being filled, not the estimate.
- Identity is the wall. Most portals need a Government Gateway, MyScotGov or council account, and the claimant signs a declaration. The agent can prepare and fill, but it cannot create a verified account or sign, so it must stop before submit.
- Income, health and disability data is special category data under UK GDPR. The product needs explicit consent, encryption and a retention limit, and the demo must use a synthetic persona.
- Submitting a real benefit claim during a demo is not acceptable. The agent must stop before submit, and any live run must use a fictional persona or a teammate's consent.
- Forms are mixed: some online, some PDF, some posted. The agent can only fill what is online, so the demo should pick schemes with real web forms.
- Means-tested schemes need income and savings evidence that a stranger does not have. The demo needs a persona whose documents we can fabricate convincingly.
- Devolved and reserved benefits overlap, and the four nations differ: some schemes are Scottish, some are DWP, and Northern Ireland uses rates relief. Getting the boundary wrong would produce confident nonsense.

## Scope

The rules cover all four nations, but the demo files in Scotland, where the sponsor and the devolved benefits are. Type one persona: a renter in Edinburgh, one child, part-time work. Live browser panes open the council's scheme, mygov.scot, a Social Security Scotland benefit and two supplier social tariff pages. The result reads: "You can claim £4,120 a year across 5 schemes. 3 forms filled, 2 need a document you don't have yet." End on a filled form, one click from submit, and the rule that grants it.

## Alternatives

- [Flat Truth](flat-truth.md): the same three tracks, and this one has a deterministic demo, but Flat Truth is not already in a sponsor's app. See Existing products.
- [Small Print Tax](small-print-tax.md): also money the household is losing, but by reading contracts rather than entitlement rules.
- [Room Radar](room-radar.md): also a form-filling agent that stops before submit, but for a much smaller problem.

## [Missing Out 2025 | Policy in Practice](https://policyinpractice.co.uk/publication/missing-out-2025/)
Published: 2025-09-12T16:58:49.000Z

## Missing Out 2025

### £24 billion of support is unclaimed

Over 7 million households are missing out on record support, driven by under claiming and new eligibility, but targeted action is beginning to turn the tide

...

## Executive summary: Missing Out 2025 reveals £24.1 billion is unclaimed

In 2025/26 an estimated £24.1 billion in income related benefits and social tariffs will go unclaimed across Great Britain. Accessing this support would help raise living standards, prevent crises and reduce pressure on public services, but it is not reaching the people who need it.

This figure reflects both welfare policy changes and improvements in how estimates are calculated. While the amount appears higher than the £22.7 billion published in 2024, differences in data and improvements to our methodology mean the two totals are not directly comparable. 

The highest unclaimed amounts are found in Universal Credit, Council Tax Support and Carer’s Allowance, showing where action could make the biggest financial difference. At the same time, the largest numbers of missed claims are linked to broadband social tariffs, water discounts and Council Tax Support, highlighting the need to improve visibility and access to support for everyday essentials.

...

To understand how things have shifted since the last report, we focused on the benefits where the data and methods are consistent across both years. We excluded Council Tax Support, Free School Meals and water support, where new modelling approaches meant the numbers could not be directly compared.

Across the remaining benefits, we found that unclaimed support increased by £2.7 billion, rising from £17.3 billion to £20 billion, a 15.6% increase. Most of that growth came from the expansion of Universal Credit (UC) as managed migration enters its final stages and the widening of eligibility for the Warm Home Discount. The number of missed UC claims rose by 16.4% while the estimated value increased by 23.4%, or £2.1 billion. For the Warm Home Discount, missed support nearly tripled (a 276% increase) after changes to eligibility rules in England and Wales.

Alongside these policy changes, we also strengthened how we build our estimates. We used more local level data, refined how we identify eligibility and updated assumptions to better reflect how support works in practice. We drew on newly published sources, including Freedom of Information responses, and used more accurate administrative definitions where possible. Some data gaps remain, but these mostly reflect how information is collected and shared, rather than a lack of transparency. Since the last report, we have also engaged closely with councils, government departments and advocacy groups, whose feedback helped us improve this year’s analysis to provide clearer, more reliable figures.

...

Tackling the £24.1 billion gap in unclaimed support is possible but requires making the system more accessible, joined up and easier to navigate. Many people are not claiming support simply because the process is unclear, complex or not designed around their needs.

## [Missing Out 2025: £24 billion of support is unclaimed](https://policyinpractice.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/MO25-24bnUnclaimed-PolicyinPractice-Sept25.pdf)

### Executive summary: Missing Out 2025 reveals £24.1 billion is unclaimed

In 2025/26 an estimated £24.1 billion in income related benefits and social tariffs will go unclaimed across Great Britain. Accessing this support would help raise living standards, prevent crises and reduce pressure on public services, but it is not reaching the people who need it.

This figure reflects both welfare policy changes and improvements in how estimates are calculated.

While the amount appears higher than the £22.7 billion published in 2024, differences in data and improvements to our methodology mean the two totals are not directly comparable.

The highest unclaimed amounts are found in Universal Credit, Council Tax Support and Carer’s Allowance, showing where action could make the biggest financial difference. At the same time, the largest numbers of missed claims are linked to broadband social tariffs, water discounts and Council Tax Support, highlighting the need to improve visibility and access to support for everyday essentials.

Table 1: Estimated value of unclaimed support, Great Britain 2025/26

| Centrally administered benefits | Missed claims Average unclaimed in a year | | £ million unclaimed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Universal Credit | 1,671,000 | £6,669 | £11,148 |
| Pension Credit | 761,000 | £2,121 | £1,615 |
| Carer’s Allowance | 553,000 | £4,252 | £2,354 |
| Child Benefit | 742,000 | £1,998 | £1,483 |
| Locally administered benefits | | | |
| Council Tax Support | 2,571,000 | £1,286 | £3,306 |
| Housing Benefits for Pensioners | 226,000 | £4,788 | £1,083 |
| Free School Meals | 123,000 | £561 | £69 |
| Healthy Start / Best Start Foods | 201,000 | £273 | £55 |
| Social tariffs and energy support | | | |
| Water Social Tariffs (incl. Water Sure) | 3,847,000 | £194 | £745 |
| Broadband | 7,537,000 | £200 | £1,508 |
| Warm Homes Discount | 4,812,000 | £150 | £722 |
| TV Licenses | 298,000 | £176 | £52 |
| Overall | 7,537,000 | £3,203 | £24,140 |

Note: The number of missed claims is rounded to the nearest thousand, so totals may not sum exactly or match when multiplying the number of claims by the average amount. The overall missed claims figure is based on the benefit with the highest number of people missing out (broadband social tariffs). Since some people miss out on multiple benefits, and different schemes count individuals or households, this is a minimum estimate. It shows that at least 7.5 million people are missing out on at least one benefit. The overall average amount missed (£3,203) is calculated by dividing the total unclaimed support (£24.1 billion) by this figure. Finally, the overall unclaimed support (in millions) is the total value considering all benefits together.

...

Across the remaining benefits, we found that unclaimed support increased by £2.7 billion, rising from £17.3 billion to £20 billion, a 15.6% increase. Most of that growth came from the expansion of Universal Credit (UC) as managed migration enters its final stages and the widening of eligibility for the Warm Home Discount. The number of missed UC claims rose by 16.4% while the estimated value increased by 23.4%, or £2.1 billion. For the Warm Home Discount, missed support nearly tripled (a 276% increase) after changes to eligibility rules in England and Wales.

...

### Introduction

Policy in Practice estimates that £24.1 billion in income related benefits and social tariffs will go unclaimed across Great Britain in 2025/26. This support could significantly improve living standards, prevent hardship, and reduce pressure on public services, but it is not reaching the people who need it.

With the cost of living still rising and household debt remaining high, many more people who are just about managing risk falling into need. 1 Our role is not only to help people access the support they are eligible for, but also to build financial resilience by giving people the confidence, stability, and tools they need to move forward and thrive, not just survive.

This figure is higher than the £22.7 billion originally published in last year’s Missing Out report however the two totals are not directly comparable.

Since 2024, both the welfare landscape and our methodology have changed. Policy developments, such as the expansion of Universal Credit through managed migration and changes to energy support eligibility, mean that more people are now missing out.

At the same time, we have strengthened our estimation methods by drawing on more local level data, refining how we assess eligibility, and incorporating new sources such as Freedom of Information responses and better data on benefits administered by the Welsh and Scottish governments. As a result, the total reflects both real increases in unmet need and improvements in how that need is measured.

To enable meaningful year on year comparisons, we compare only the benefits where methods remained consistent across both reports. This shows a 15.6% increase in unclaimed support across those benefits, rising from £17.3 billion to £20 billion. Most of this growth was due to a sharp increase in missed Universal Credit claims and a major expansion of eligibility for the Warm Home Discount.

...

Our estimates combine official data from central government, local authorities and regulators with published or inferred take up rates to estimate how many people are likely eligible but not claiming.

For each benefit, we multiply the number of missed claims by a typical award, adjusting for policy changes, uprating and the fact that lower-value claims are less likely to be made. This method captures both the scale and the financial value of missed support across national, local and utility administered schemes.

We do not include disability benefits or discretionary local schemes in this total as these require individual assessments that are difficult to model reliably. However, when these forms of support are considered, the true level of unclaimed assistance is likely to exceed £30 billion. Full methodological details can be found in the Technical Appendix.

## [Seven million households missing out on benefits and support](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c5yv0e9yjexo)
Published: 2025-09-12T23:55:16.000Z

New analysis suggests seven million households are missing out on £24bn of financial help and support because of unclaimed benefits and social tariffs.

...

## Unclaimed benefits increasing

In its latest report, Policy in Practice estimates that £24.1bn in benefits and social tariffs will go unclaimed in 2025-26.

It previously estimated that £23bn would go unclaimed in 2024-25, and £19bn the year before that, although this year's calculations are more detailed than ever before.

## [🚨 Our brand new Missing Out 2025 report is out and it has already been featured on BBC Breakfast, ITV and Money Box 📺 | Policy in Practice](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/REDACTED)
Published: 2025-09-16T00:00:00.000Z

🚨 Our brand new  Missing Out 2025 report is out and it has already been featured on BBC Breakfast, ITV and Money Box 📺

It shows £24.1 billion of support is going unclaimed 💸

Over 7 million households are missing out, but action to close the gap is working:

🏠 Local authorities using our LIFT platform have helped 62,000 households to become better off by over £77 million a year. On top of this, people will continue to get support each year, making the lifetime impact of LIFT over £500 million.

📱 Every day, thousands of people use our Better Off Calculator through GOV.UK and over 230,000 people identify £1.4 billion in unclaimed support annually using the Better Off Calculator. Those eligible identified almost £6,000 in extra annual income.

## [Now: Social Security system is ‘too complex, fragmented and passive’, with more than £24 billion going unclaimed in 2025 - Rightsnet](https://www.rightsnet.org.uk/now/post/68188)
Published: 2024-01-01T00:00:00.000Z

In a new report, Policy in Practice has found that £24.1 billion in benefits and support is going unclaimed in 2025.

Key findings include:

- the total for 2025 is a new high, up from £19 billion in 2023 and £23 billion in 2024;
- almost half of this (£11.1 billion) relates to unclaimed universal credit;
- more than 7 million households are missing out on the help they’re entitled to, including more than 1.7 million working-age families and 750,000 pensioners; and
- while targeted actions across central government, local government, private and voluntary sectors are making a difference, key barriers to take-up include people's lack of awareness, the complexity of the system and stigma and negative perceptions linked to claiming social security.

## [£24 billion of support is unclaimed: new “Missing Out” report](https://www.disabilityrightsuk.org/news/%C2%A324-billion-support-unclaimed-new-%E2%80%9Cmissing-out%E2%80%9D-report)
Published: 2025-09-22T00:00:00.000Z

In 2025/26 an estimated £24.1 billion in income related benefits and social tariffs will go unclaimed across Great Britain, according to a new report from Policy in Practice. 

Accessing this support would help raise living standards, prevent crises and reduce pressure on public services, but it is not reaching the people who need it.

This figure reflects both welfare policy changes and improvements in how estimates are calculated. 

The highest unclaimed amounts are found in: 

- universal credit
- council tax support 
- carer’s allowance

showing where action could make the biggest financial difference. 

At the same time, the largest numbers of missed claims are linked to broadband social tariffs, water discounts and council tax support, highlighting the need to improve visibility and access to support for everyday essentials.

## [The essential role online calculators play in closing the £24 billion unclaimed support gap | Policy in Practice](https://policyinpractice.co.uk/blog/the-essential-role-online-calculators-play-in-closing-the-24-billion-unclaimed-support-gap/)
Published: 2026-01-29T10:42:33.000Z

An estimated £24 billion of financial support goes unclaimed every year. That figure, now widely referenced across the sector, comes from our annual Missing Out analysis.

One of the main reasons for this gap is that many people do not know what benefits or other financial support they are entitled to, leading to at least 8 million households missing out on vital support. Other factors such as system complexity and stigma make the problem worse but lack of awareness is the starting point. You cannot claim support you don’t know exists.

## [DWP cry about benefit fraud but billions go unclaimed](https://www.thecanary.co/uk/analysis/2025/09/19/labour-claims-24-billion-of-benefits-went-unclaimed-last-year-but-the-way-they-talk-about-benefits-is-why/)
Published: 2025-09-19T15:04:14.000Z

Police In Practice produces a yearly Missing Out report, which projects how many people won’t claim benefits. It has calculated that in the financial year 2025/26 £24.1bn will go unclaimed in a range of means-tested benefits, meaning that over 7 million households will go without vital support.

## Data sources

The rules come from four tiers, each with a different reliability and access method.

- **National law and guidance.** GOV.UK's Content and Search APIs return published pages as JSON without a key, and legislation.gov.uk has an API for the statutes and regulations behind them. Social Security Scotland and mygov.scot publish the devolved benefits, and nidirect publishes the Northern Ireland equivalents.
- **Local schemes.** About 350 councils run their own council tax reduction scheme: 296 billing authorities in England, 32 in Scotland and 22 in Wales. Each publishes a scheme document and its own application form. Local welfare assistance schemes are separate again and vary by council. Northern Ireland has no council tax; help with rates is Rate Relief and Rate Rebate, run by Land & Property Services and applied for through nidirect.
- **Supplier schemes.** Ofcom publishes the list of broadband and phone social tariffs with prices and coverage. Water companies publish their own reduction schemes, and the Warm Home Discount is administered through energy suppliers.
- **Eligibility engines.** EntitledTo, Inbest and Policy in Practice sell APIs that already encode Universal Credit and the legacy means-tested benefits, including the earnings taper, childcare and housing elements. Inbest is the awkward one, because it is the product already inside the Bank of Scotland app.

How the data is used:

- A rules store holds one entry per scheme: jurisdiction, eligibility conditions, award formula, evidence needed, application URL, source URL and effective date. Every entry carries a quotation from the source, so the product can show why a figure is owed.
- An ingestion job fetches the official pages and has a model extract them into that schema. A deterministic evaluator computes eligibility and amounts. The model never does arithmetic and never invents a threshold.
- A re-fetch job diffs the pages and flags changes, because rates change each April and council schemes change annually.
- A postcode router picks the nation, then the council, then the schemes. The four nations do not share a system: Scotland has devolved benefits that England and Wales do not, and Northern Ireland uses rates relief.
- The claim layer is one adapter per portal, because the fields, login and evidence upload differ. Identity is the wall: most portals need a Government Gateway, MyScotGov or council account, and the claimant signs a declaration. The agent can fill and stop; it cannot create a verified account or sign.

The honest scope: the rules layer can cover all four nations, but the form layer cannot cover 350 councils in a weekend. The buildable version is all-UK rules with depth in Scotland, where the sponsor and the devolved benefits are, and a small number of real form adapters.

## Tracks it could serve

- Bank of Scotland: strong. This is the most direct fit of any idea so far. The brief is about everyday trade-offs between cost, time, convenience and sustainability, and this is money a household is already entitled to, with no trade-off except the effort of claiming. "Better" is defined by the household: more money, or the same money for less work.
- Wordsmith: strong. It is legal and administrative work, which Wordsmith prefers, and the workflow is longer than a read-only report: read circumstances, test them against a dozen rule sets, pick the schemes that apply, gather evidence, fill several unrelated forms with different fields, and stop before submit. Tokens, model and time should be shown, since Wordsmith also judges those.
- G-Research: strong. The hidden thing is money sitting unclaimed, found by cross-checking a household against eligibility rules that are scattered across councils and agencies, and it enables a claim worth hundreds or thousands a year. It answers the brief's three questions without needing a scrape of a site that may block us.
- HRT: weak. There is no market data and no real-time signal. At most, the entitlement rules could be modelled as a decision tree over a synthetic population, which is not what the track asks for.

## Challenges it could use

- Gemini API: reading council schemes and application forms, and driving the browser agent.
- Auth0: keeping a household's details and saved claims between sessions.
- Vultr: hosting the backend and the demo, separate from the browser runner.

## Open problems

These are unchecked, apart from the market check above.

- The total unclaimed is reported in the billions of pounds a year, but the figure, its source and its date are unverified. Do not cite a number until it is checked.
- The rules are genuinely complex and differ by council: about 350 councils run their own council tax reduction scheme, and the schemes change yearly. A wrong answer here is harmful in a way a wrong rent estimate is not, so the product should show which rule produced each figure and link to the source.
- Universal Credit is a means test with an earnings taper, childcare and housing elements. Rebuilding it is not a 24-hour job, and an LLM doing the arithmetic will be wrong. Use an eligibility engine, or hand-code a small set of schemes for the demo.
- Differentiation is the main risk. See Existing products: the Bank of Scotland app already contains Inbest's calculator, so the demo must show the forms being filled, not the estimate.
- Identity is the wall. Most portals need a Government Gateway, MyScotGov or council account, and the claimant signs a declaration. The agent can prepare and fill, but it cannot create a verified account or sign, so it must stop before submit.
- Income, health and disability data is special category data under UK GDPR. The product needs explicit consent, encryption and a retention limit, and the demo must use a synthetic persona.
- Submitting a real benefit claim during a demo is not acceptable. The agent must stop before submit, and any live run must use a fictional persona or a teammate's consent.
- Forms are mixed: some online, some PDF, some posted. The agent can only fill what is online, so the demo should pick schemes with real web forms.
- Means-tested schemes need income and savings evidence that a stranger does not have. The demo needs a persona whose documents we can fabricate convincingly.
- Devolved and reserved benefits overlap, and the four nations differ: some schemes are Scottish, some are DWP, and Northern Ireland uses rates relief. Getting the boundary wrong would produce confident nonsense.

## Scope

The rules cover all four nations, but the demo files in Scotland, where the sponsor and the devolved benefits are. Type one persona: a renter in Edinburgh, one child, part-time work. Live browser panes open the council's scheme, mygov.scot, a Social Security Scotland benefit and two supplier social tariff pages. The result reads: "You can claim £4,120 a year across 5 schemes. 3 forms filled, 2 need a document you don't have yet." End on a filled form, one click from submit, and the rule that grants it.

## Alternatives

- [Flat Truth](flat-truth.md): the same three tracks, and this one has a deterministic demo, but Flat Truth is not already in a sponsor's app. See Existing products.
- [Small Print Tax](small-print-tax.md): also money the household is losing, but by reading contracts rather than entitlement rules.
- [Room Radar](room-radar.md): also a form-filling agent that stops before submit, but for a much smaller problem.

## Executive summary: Missing Out 2025 reveals £24.1 billion is unclaimed

In 2025/26 an estimated £24.1 billion in income related benefits and social tariffs will go unclaimed across Great Britain. Accessing this support would help raise living standards, prevent crises and reduce pressure on public services, but it is not reaching the people who need it.

This figure reflects both welfare policy changes and improvements in how estimates are calculated. While the amount appears higher than the £22.7 billion published in 2024, differences in data and improvements to our methodology mean the two totals are not directly comparable. 

The highest unclaimed amounts are found in Universal Credit, Council Tax Support and Carer’s Allowance, showing where action could make the biggest financial difference. At the same time, the largest numbers of missed claims are linked to broadband social tariffs, water discounts and Council Tax Support, highlighting the need to improve visibility and access to support for everyday essentials.

...

To understand how things have shifted since the last report, we focused on the benefits where the data and methods are consistent across both years. We excluded Council Tax Support, Free School Meals and water support, where new modelling approaches meant the numbers could not be directly compared.

Across the remaining benefits, we found that unclaimed support increased by £2.7 billion, rising from £17.3 billion to £20 billion, a 15.6% increase. Most of that growth came from the expansion of Universal Credit (UC) as managed migration enters its final stages and the widening of eligibility for the Warm Home Discount. The number of missed UC claims rose by 16.4% while the estimated value increased by 23.4%, or £2.1 billion. For the Warm Home Discount, missed support nearly tripled (a 276% increase) after changes to eligibility rules in England and Wales.

Alongside these policy changes, we also strengthened how we build our estimates. We drew on newly published sources, including Freedom of Information responses, and used more accurate administrative definitions where possible. Some data gaps remain, but these mostly reflect how information is collected and shared, rather than a lack of transparency. Since the last report, we have also engaged closely with councils, government departments and advocacy groups, whose feedback helped us improve this year’s analysis to provide clearer, more reliable figures.

...

 Same broadband, lower price 

 A social tariff is the same broadband, delivered the same way, at a lower price — not a poorer service. If you qualify, there is no catch and no fee to leave, so there is little reason not to ask. 

## What Ofcom says you get

- • Switching to your own provider’s: If your own provider offers a social tariff, Ofcom says you can switch to it at any time, free of charge.
- • Leaving one: Ofcom says you won’t pay a fee to leave a social tariff before the end of the contract.
- • Moving to another provider: If your provider doesn’t offer one, you can move to a provider that does — but Ofcom only says your current provider “might” let you leave without an exit fee. Ask before you commit.
- • Mid-contract rises: The price won’t go up mid-contract — you pay what you agreed at the start.
- • Set-up costs: Set-up costs should be next to nothing, and your provider should tell you about any before you sign up.
- • New customers: You don’t have to be an existing customer — if your provider has no social tariff you can switch to one that does.
- • Whose name it’s in: The person receiving the benefit needs to be the main person on the contract.
- • Coverage: Providers might not cover every address in the regions listed, so check the provider’s own site for your postcode.

## [Back to school financial support - Social Security Scotland](https://www.socialsecurity.gov.scot/news/2026/07/back-to-school-support)
Published: 2026-07-28T09:00:00.000Z

Support for nursery-aged children 

For families with children aged between two years and three years and six months old, the Best Start Grant Early Learning Payment of £331.95 can help with the costs of toys, books, clothing and other items that support a child's development. There is no requirement to take up a place at nursery to qualify for this payment. Families receiving Scottish Child Payment and are eligible for this payment will be paid automatically, there is no need to apply.

...

Help for all ages - families with children 16 years and under 

Scottish Child Payment is available to families with children under 16 and provides £112.80 every four weeks for every eligible child. It's designed to help with the everyday costs of raising a family and can make a significant difference to household finances throughout the year – not just at back-to-school time.

## [Our benefits - Social Security Scotland](https://www.socialsecurity.gov.scot/our-benefits?preview-token=REDACTED

## Five family payments

- Best Start Grant and Best Start Foods

- Pregnancy and Baby Payment – a one-off payment of up to £796.65 from 24 weeks in pregnancy up until a baby turns 6 months for families who get certain benefits.
- Early Learning Payment – a one-off payment of £331.95 when a child is between two and three years and six months for families who get certain benefits.
- School Age Payment – a one-off payment of £331.95 when a child would normally start primary one for families who get certain benefits.
- Best Start Foods – a pre-paid card from pregnancy up to when a child turns three for families on certain benefits to help buy healthy food.
- Scottish Child Payment - a payment of £112.80 every four weeks to help towards the costs of looking after each child under 16 for families who get certain benefits.

## [Best Start Grant and Best Start Foods](https://www.mygov.scot/best-start-grant-best-start-foods)

10 Aug 2026

Best Start Grant and Best Start Foods are payments that help towards the costs of being pregnant or looking after a child.

When to apply for different family payments

| When you can apply | You may be able to get |
| --- | --- |
| Apply as soon as you know you're pregnant, or up until your child turns 3 years old. | Best Start Foods |
| Apply after 24 weeks of pregnancy to help prepare for your baby’s arrival, or after your baby is born. | Best Start Grant – Pregnancy and Baby Payment |
| Apply when your child is aged between 2 and 3 years 6 months old. | Best Start Grant – Early Learning Payment |
| Apply when your child is first old enough to start primary school. When you should apply depends on when your child was born. You need to apply in the year that your child is first old enough to start school. | Best Start Grant – School Age Payment |

These are the 5 family payments, along with Scottish Child Payment, you may be able to get from Social Security Scotland. You can apply for them all using the same form. You'll get separate letters to let you know whether you'll get each payment.

If you live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, you cannot get Best Start Grant or Best Start Foods. You can apply for Sure Start Maternity Grant and Healthy Start Payments.

## About Best Start Grant

The 3 Best Start Grant payments are:

### Pregnancy and Baby Payment 

Pregnancy and Baby Payment helps with the costs of having a baby. You can apply for this payment during pregnancy to help prepare for your baby's arrival, or after your baby is born.

You can get Pregnancy and Baby Payment any time after you have reached the end of the 24th week of pregnancy until the day your baby is 6 months old. If your baby is born before 24 weeks, you can apply from this date up to the day your baby is 6 months old. If you've taken over looking after a child, for example, if you've adopted, you can apply up to the day before the child's first birthday.

You can get Pregnancy and Baby Payment for multiple children, as long as each child is the right age when you apply. The amount paid for each child will be different if you have more than one child.

You'll get a Pregnancy and Baby Payment of £796.65 for your first child. Your first child is your oldest child under 16. This includes a stepchild, if you have one. It also includes any child you've taken over looking after, for example, if you've adopted, or kinship care.

This will change to a payment of £398.35 for any child that comes after your first. For example, your second or third child, or any child after these.

You can use the payment for anything you need. This could include:

- pregnancy clothes
- a pram
- a cot
- baby clothes
- toys

#### Extra support

In some circumstances, you may be able to get extra support for a child that’s not your first. You may get the £796.65 payment if: 

- you or your partner became responsible for your other child or children when they were over 12 months old, and did not give birth to them 

- you had to leave your home with your other child or children because of domestic abuse by your partner or ex-partner 

- you're a refugee or have humanitarian protection and your other child or children were born before you arrived in the UK 

- you have leave to reside in the UK under a resettlement scheme, such as, but not limited to, the Afghanistan or Ukraine schemes and your other child or children were born before you arrived in the UK

...

- you’re a British or Irish national or have leave to remain and have returned to the UK due to ‘leave now’ guidance or the UK government has evacuated you back to the UK, and your other children were born before you returned

...

You cannot get the Pregnancy and Baby Payment if you’ve already got the Sure Start Maternity Grant for the same baby 

#### Applying for a multiple birth

If you apply for twins and have no other children under 16

| Your payment for 1st twin | Your payment for 2nd twin | Extra payment for twins | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| £796.65 | £398.35 | £398.35 | £1,593.35 |

If you apply for twins and have other children under 16

| Your payment for 1st twin | Your payment for 2nd twin | Extra payment for twins | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| £398.35 | £398.35 | £398.35 | £1,195.05 |

##### If you apply for triplets

If you have triplets, you'll be paid an extra £398.35 on top of what you get for twins. This means you'd get either:

- £1,991.70 if you do not have any other children under 16
- £1,593.40 if you do have other children under 16

You can still get the Pregnancy and Baby Payment part of Best Start Grant for a baby that was stillborn or died after they were born. If you're paid when you're pregnant, and your baby is stillborn or dies later, you will not need to pay any money back. If you apply after a stillbirth or death, you can apply up to 6 months after the baby's birth date.

### Early Learning Payment 

If your application is successful you'll get £331.95 to help with the costs of early learning. You can get the payment when your child is aged between 2 years old and 3 years and 6 months old. To get this payment your child does not need to go to nursery.

You can get Early Learning Payment for multiple children, as long as each child is the right age when you apply.

You can spend this money on anything you need for your child at this age. This could include:

- clothes
- toys
- trips to new places

### School Age Payment 

School Age Payment is a payment of £331.95 per child. It helps with the costs of preparing for school when your child is first old enough to start primary school.

You can get the payment for multiple children, as long as each child is the right age when you apply.

To get a payment, your child does not have to take up a place at school. You'll still need to apply in the year that your child is first old enough to start school, if:

- you're deferring when your child starts school
- your child is not going to school

When you need to apply for the School Age Payment depends on when your child was born:

When to apply for School Age Payment

| Your child's date of birth | When you can apply |
| --- | --- |
| Between 1 March 2021 and 28 February 2022 | Between 1 June 2026 and 28 February 2027 |
| Between 1 March 2022 and 28 February 2023 | Between 1 June 2027 and 29 February 2028 |

The application dates for children born between 1 March 2020 and 28 February 2021 have now passed. You cannot apply for a child outside of these application dates.

You can spend this money on anything you need for your child at this age. This could include:

- clothes
- school trips
- stationery for school

The School Age Payment has not replaced the School Clothing Grant. The School Age Payment is a new payment and it does not affect payments of the School Clothing Grant in any way. If you want to apply for both, you can.

Social Security Scotland usually only make each of the payments once for the same child. If responsibility for the child changes, they may make extra payments to the person who’s now responsible for the child. For example, if a child moves to live with a different kinship carer or adoptive parent within the same application window.

...

Best Start Foods is paid every 4 weeks. The payments are:

- £22.40 during pregnancy (you’ll get the same amount whether you’re having one or more babies)
- £44.80 for each child from birth until they’re one year old
- £22.40 for each child aged between one and 3 years old

- Best Start grant pregnancy and baby payment from £767.50 to £796.65 (or from £383.75 to £398.35 if another child under 16 in the family)
- Best Start grant early learning payment from £319.80 to £331.95
- Best Start grant school age payment from £319.80 to £331.95 (available from 1 June)

Entitlement to any amount of universal credit is enough to qualify for these payments. These payments are not included in the benefit cap and are payable as well as universal credit child elements and child benefit.

## [Important changes to Best Start Grant Pregnancy and Baby Payment - Social Security Scotland](https://www.socialsecurity.gov.scot/news/2026/03/new-exceptions-to-higher-pregnancy-and-baby-payment)
Published: 2026-03-17T10:15:00.000Z

From 18 March 2026, the rules for Best Start Grant Pregnancy and Baby Payment will change.

From 18 March 2026, the rules for Best Start Grant Pregnancy and Baby Payment will change. These changes only affect a small number of people, but they may be people you support. 

This article explains what is changing, who these changes apply to, and how to help clients access the right support. 

About Pregnancy and Baby Payment 

Pregnancy and Baby Payment is a one-off payment to help with the cost of pregnancy or having a new baby. Families can apply from 24 weeks pregnant until the baby is 6 months old. 

Payment amounts are: 

- £767.50 for a first child (£796.65 from April 2026) 

- £383.75 for later children (£398.35 from April 2026) 

Some families may already be eligible for the higher payment amount, even if the baby is not their first child. Further information on extra support can be found here: Best Start Grant and Best Start Foods - mygov.scot 

Who the upcoming changes apply to 

From 18 March 2026, people will also be able to receive the higher amount if all their other children were born before they arrived in the UK, including: 

1. People who have been granted leave under a safe and legal humanitarian immigration route, either inside or outside the immigration rules, all of whose other children were born before they arrived. 

2. People who are a British or Irish national, or people with leave to remain, who had to return to the UK in an emergency. 

This includes returning because of: 

- official “leave now” guidance, or 

- a UK Government evacuation. 

3. Individuals arriving from the Middle East may also be covered by these exemptions, including people who were residing in Oman before 4 March and who arrive in the UK before 3 September 2026. 

These are the only groups affected by the March 2026 change. 

 All other rules remain the same.

...

If someone fits into one of the three groups above, they may now be able to receive the higher payment — even if the new baby is not their first child.

## [How much are the Best Start Grant payments - Citizens Advice](https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/scotland/benefits/help-if-on-a-low-income/best-start-grant/best-start/how-much-are-the-best-start-grant-payments/)

The Best Start Grant is a Scottish benefit to help parents and carers on low incomes with the costs of looking after children. There are 3 different payments, which you can apply for as your child gets older.

## How much is the School Age Payment

The School Age Payment is a one-off payment of £331.95. It increased from £319.80 on 1 April 2026.

There's no limit on the number of children in a family that you can get the payment for.

## How much is the Early Learning Payment

The Early Learning Payment is a one-off payment of £331.95. It increased from £319.80 on 1 April 2026.

There's no limit on the number of children in a family that you can get the payment for.

## How much is the Pregnancy and Baby Payment

There are 2 rates of Pregnancy and Baby Payment.

You'll usually get:

- £796.65 for a first child
- £398.35 for a second or later child.

In some cases, you'll get the higher payment even if you're applying for a second or later child.

You'll also get more money if you're expecting more than 1 baby - for example, you're having twins.

If you applied before 1 April 2025, you'll get £767.50 for a first child and £383.75 for a second or later child.

### If this is your first child 

You'll get £796.65 if the baby is your first child.

You'll get this payment if there's no other child under 16 living in your household for whom you're responsible. You're usually responsible for a child if you're getting Child Benefit or the child element of Universal Credit for them.

For example, if you have a 17-year-old stepson living with you and then you have a baby, you'll get a Pregnancy and Baby Payment of £796.65 for your baby. This is because your stepson is over 16 and so is not treated as your first child.

### If this is your second or later child or you already have a child living in your family 

You'll usually get £398.35 if the baby is not your first child.

If you're responsible for another child under 16 who is living in your household, they'll be counted as a first child. You're usually responsible for a child if you're getting Child Benefit or the child element of Universal Credit for them.

For example, if you have a 10-year-old stepson living with you and then you have a baby, you'll get a Pregnancy and Baby Payment of £398.35 for your baby. This is because your stepson is treated as your first child.

There's no cap on the number of children you can get a Pregnancy and Baby Payment for.

#### When you can get the higher payment

You can get the higher payment of £796.65, even if it's not for your first child, if you:

- have other children who are not your own and you took responsibility for them when they were older than 12 months old
- were forced to leave your home with your children due to domestic abuse
- have refugee status, humanitarian protection or leave under a UK government humanitarian scheme and your other children were born before coming to the UK.

You can select which circumstance applies to you when you apply for the payment.

### If you have twins or more than 1 baby in the same pregnancy 

If you're expecting more than 1 baby, for example twins or triplets, you can get an extra £398.35. This is called a 'multiple pregnancy supplement'.

For example, if you have twins and the eldest of them is your first child, you'll get £1,566.35 in total. This is made up of:

- £796.65 for the first twin
- £398.35 for the second twin
- £398.35 for the multiple pregnancy supplement.

If you have twins and they're not your first children, you'll get £1,195.05 in total. This is:

- £398.35 for the first twin
- £398.35 for the second twin
- £398.35 for the multiple pregnancy supplement.

## How the payments are made

The payments will usually be made into your bank, building society or credit union account.

You can choose for the payment to be made into someone else's account, such as your partner's account. You should always make sure that you'll be able to get the money to spend on your child. If you want to do this, put the other person's bank account details into the 'Payment details' section on the application form. 

Find out how long it will take to get the payment.

These are the 5 family payments, along with Scottish Child Payment, you may be able to get from Social Security Scotland. You can apply for them all using the same form. You'll get separate letters to let you know whether you'll get each payment.

If you live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, you cannot get Best Start Grant or Best Start Foods. You can apply for Sure Start Maternity Grant and Healthy Start Payments.

## About Best Start Grant

The 3 Best Start Grant payments are:

### Pregnancy and Baby Payment 

Pregnancy and Baby Payment helps with the costs of having a baby. You can apply for this payment during pregnancy to help prepare for your baby's arrival, or after your baby is born.

You can get Pregnancy and Baby Payment any time after you have reached the end of the 24th week of pregnancy until the day your baby is 6 months old. If your baby is born before 24 weeks, you can apply from this date up to the day your baby is 6 months old. If you've taken over looking after a child, for example, if you've adopted, you can apply up to the day before the child's first birthday.

You can get Pregnancy and Baby Payment for multiple children, as long as each child is the right age when you apply. The amount paid for each child will be different if you have more than one child.

You'll get a Pregnancy and Baby Payment of £796.65 for your first child. Your first child is your oldest child under 16. This includes a stepchild, if you have one. It also includes any child you've taken over looking after, for example, if you've adopted, or kinship care.

This will change to a payment of £398.35 for any child that comes after your first. For example, your second or third child, or any child after these.

You can use the payment for anything you need. This could include:

- pregnancy clothes
- a pram

- baby clothes
- toys

- you or your partner became responsible for your other child or children when they were over 12 months old, and did not give birth to them 

- you had to leave your home with your other child or children because of domestic abuse by your partner or ex-partner 

- you're a refugee or have humanitarian protection and your other child or children were born before you arrived in the UK

### Early Learning Payment 

If your application is successful you'll get £331.95 to help with the costs of early learning. You can get the payment when your child is aged between 2 years old and 3 years and 6 months old. To get this payment your child does not need to go to nursery.

You can get Early Learning Payment for multiple children, as long as each child is the right age when you apply.

### School Age Payment 

School Age Payment is a payment of £331.95 per child. It helps with the costs of preparing for school when your child is first old enough to start primary school.

You can get the payment for multiple children, as long as each child is the right age when you apply.

To get a payment, your child does not have to take up a place at school. You'll still need to apply in the year that your child is first old enough to start school, if:

- you're deferring when your child starts school
- your child is not going to school

When you need to apply for the School Age Payment depends on when your child was born:

When to apply for School Age Payment

| --- | --- |

| Between 1 March 2022 and 28 February 2023 | Between 1 June 2027 and 29 February 2028 |

The application dates for children born between 1 March 2020 and 28 February 2021 have now passed. You cannot apply for a child outside of these application dates.

You can spend this money on anything you need for your child at this age. This could include:

- clothes

- stationery for school

If responsibility for the child changes, they may make extra payments to the person who’s now responsible for the child. ## [Important changes to Best Start Grant Pregnancy and Baby Payment - Social Security Scotland](https://www.socialsecurity.gov.scot/news/2026/03/new-exceptions-to-higher-pregnancy-and-baby-payment)
Published: 2026-03-17T10:15:00.000Z

From 18 March 2026, the rules for Best Start Grant Pregnancy and Baby Payment will change.

From 18 March 2026, the rules for Best Start Grant Pregnancy and Baby Payment will change. These changes only affect a small number of people, but they may be people you support. 

This article explains what is changing, who these changes apply to, and how to help clients access the right support. 

About Pregnancy and Baby Payment 

Pregnancy and Baby Payment is a one-off payment to help with the cost of pregnancy or having a new baby. Families can apply from 24 weeks pregnant until the baby is 6 months old. 

Payment amounts are: 

- £767.50 for a first child (£796.65 from April 2026) 

- £383.75 for later children (£398.35 from April 2026) 

Some families may already be eligible for the higher payment amount, even if the baby is not their first child. Further information on extra support can be found here: Best Start Grant and Best Start Foods - mygov.scot 

Who the upcoming changes apply to 

From 18 March 2026, people will also be able to receive the higher amount if all their other children were born before they arrived in the UK, including: 

1. People who have been granted leave under a safe and legal humanitarian immigration route, either inside or outside the immigration rules, all of whose other children were born before they arrived. 

2. People who are a British or Irish national, or people with leave to remain, who had to return to the UK in an emergency. 

This includes returning because of: 

- official “leave now” guidance, or 

- a UK Government evacuation. 

3. Individuals arriving from the Middle East may also be covered by these exemptions, including people who were residing in Oman before 4 March and who arrive in the UK before 3 September 2026. 

These are the only groups affected by the March 2026 change. 

 All other rules remain the same.

...

If someone fits into one of the three groups above, they may now be able to receive the higher payment — even if the new baby is not their first child.

## [How much are the Best Start Grant payments - Citizens Advice](https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/scotland/benefits/help-if-on-a-low-income/best-start-grant/best-start/how-much-are-the-best-start-grant-payments/)

The Best Start Grant is a Scottish benefit to help parents and carers on low incomes with the costs of looking after children. There are 3 different payments, which you can apply for as your child gets older.

## How much is the School Age Payment

The School Age Payment is a one-off payment of £331.95. It increased from £319.80 on 1 April 2026.

There's no limit on the number of children in a family that you can get the payment for.

## How much is the Early Learning Payment

The Early Learning Payment is a one-off payment of £331.95. It increased from £319.80 on 1 April 2026.

There's no limit on the number of children in a family that you can get the payment for.

## How much is the Pregnancy and Baby Payment

There are 2 rates of Pregnancy and Baby Payment.

You'll usually get:

- £796.65 for a first child
- £398.35 for a second or later child.

In some cases, you'll get the higher payment even if you're applying for a second or later child.

You'll also get more money if you're expecting more than 1 baby - for example, you're having twins.

If you applied before 1 April 2025, you'll get £767.50 for a first child and £383.75 for a second or later child.

### If this is your first child 

You'll get £796.65 if the baby is your first child.

You'll get this payment if there's no other child under 16 living in your household for whom you're responsible. You're usually responsible for a child if you're getting Child Benefit or the child element of Universal Credit for them.

For example, if you have a 17-year-old stepson living with you and then you have a baby, you'll get a Pregnancy and Baby Payment of £796.65 for your baby. This is because your stepson is over 16 and so is not treated as your first child.

### If this is your second or later child or you already have a child living in your family 

You'll usually get £398.35 if the baby is not your first child.

If you're responsible for another child under 16 who is living in your household, they'll be counted as a first child. You're usually responsible for a child if you're getting Child Benefit or the child element of Universal Credit for them.

For example, if you have a 10-year-old stepson living with you and then you have a baby, you'll get a Pregnancy and Baby Payment of £398.35 for your baby. This is because your stepson is treated as your first child.

There's no cap on the number of children you can get a Pregnancy and Baby Payment for.

#### When you can get the higher payment

You can get the higher payment of £796.65, even if it's not for your first child, if you:

- have other children who are not your own and you took responsibility for them when they were older than 12 months old
- were forced to leave your home with your children due to domestic abuse
- have refugee status, humanitarian protection or leave under a UK government humanitarian scheme and your other children were born before coming to the UK.

You can select which circumstance applies to you when you apply for the payment.

### If you have twins or more than 1 baby in the same pregnancy 

If you're expecting more than 1 baby, for example twins or triplets, you can get an extra £398.35. This is called a 'multiple pregnancy supplement'.

For example, if you have twins and the eldest of them is your first child, you'll get £1,566.35 in total. This is made up of:

- £796.65 for the first twin
- £398.35 for the second twin
- £398.35 for the multiple pregnancy supplement.

If you have twins and they're not your first children, you'll get £1,195.05 in total. This is:

- £398.35 for the first twin
- £398.35 for the second twin
- £398.35 for the multiple pregnancy supplement.

## How the payments are made

The payments will usually be made into your bank, building society or credit union account.

You can choose for the payment to be made into someone else's account, such as your partner's account. You should always make sure that you'll be able to get the money to spend on your child. If you want to do this, put the other person's bank account details into the 'Payment details' section on the application form. 

Find out how long it will take to get the payment.
